findings.title: Unbounded memory allocation in readBytes() allows denial of service
findings.evidence: Method readBytes() allocates byte array of size (int)contentLength without reasonable limit. contentLength is read as unsigned int from attacker-controlled stream via unsignedExtend(in.readInt()), allowing values up to Integer.MAX_VALUE - 1 (2,147,483,647). Line 87-88 allocates: new byte[(int)contentLength].
findings.impact: Denial of service via heap exhaustion. Attacker can send crafted AMQP message with contentLength=Integer.MAX_VALUE-1, causing allocation of 2GB heap memory. Multiple requests exhaust available memory and crash JVM with OutOfMemoryError.
findings.preconditions: Attacker can send crafted AMQP messages to the client, either by controlling the broker or via man-in-the-middle. In typical setups, only trusted brokers send messages, but library should be defensively programmed.
findings.recommendation: Add configurable maximum size limit for byte arrays, with sensible default (e.g., 128 MB). Check contentLength against limit before allocation. Example: if(contentLength > MAX_SIZE) throw new MalformedFrameException().
traceability: CWE-770: Allocation of Resources Without Limits or Throttling

triage.reason: No compensating control. Method directly allocates byte array without size validation or quota enforcement.
contentLength is read directly from untrusted stream via in.readInt() on line 86, converted to unsigned via unsignedExtend(). Attacker fully controls this value.
The allocation itself (new byte[(int)contentLength]) is the dangerous sink. Allocating 2GB of memory from untrusted input causes OutOfMemoryError and denial of service.
Boundary is crossed: attacker sends crafted AMQP message to client, causing client's JVM to exhaust memory.

findings.title: Timestamp multiplication overflow in readTimestamp() — informational only
findings.evidence: Method readTimestamp() multiplies long value by 1000 without overflow check: return new Date(in.readLong()*1000). When in.readLong() value exceeds Long.MAX_VALUE/1000 (~9.2 billion), multiplication overflows to incorrect value.
findings.impact: Integer overflow causes Date to be constructed with incorrect timestamp. However, since the timestamp value itself is attacker-controlled, this grants no capability beyond what the attacker already had (ability to send any timestamp).
findings.preconditions: Attacker sends AMQP message with timestamp field value > Long.MAX_VALUE/1000.
findings.recommendation: Add overflow check for defense-in-depth: use Math.multiplyExact(timestamp, 1000L) which throws ArithmeticException on overflow, or check if(timestamp > Long.MAX_VALUE/1000) before multiplication. This prevents silent truncation of timestamp values.

triage.reason: Timestamp is read directly from untrusted stream via in.readLong() on line 269
The sink (Date constructor) is not dangerous. An incorrect Date object does not grant the attacker new capability since they already controlled the input timestamp value.

findings.limits: Impact is purely defensive. The attacker already possessed the ability to send any timestamp value. Overflowing it creates an incorrect Date, but the attacker already could have sent a different correct timestamp.
